overview: ASCEND’s UAS work connects aircraft engineering with atmospheric research. Fixed-wing aircraft are intended to measure horizontal variability, while multirotor aircraft support detailed vertical profiles in the lower atmosphere.

Teams will integrate sensors and data systems, test their platforms, and evaluate measurements alongside balloon and surface observations. The aircraft resources below support the engineering skills needed for that work.

Every UAS team will fly the ASCEND Logger, a small PCB that records GPS position, pressure, temperature, and humidity, with an I2C port for a PM2.5 air-quality sensor. Logger setup and mounting guides are in development.
The Flight Training collection brings together simulator practice, aircraft references, and a fixed-wing launch demonstration. Additional learning-to-fly materials will be added here.

description: Download the circuit boards behind ASCEND hardware: Fusion designs, schematics, board layouts, parts lists, and Gerbers for ordering your own boards.
overview: Each ASCEND circuit board is published as a complete design kit, so your team can study how it works, change it, or have your own boards made.

Every kit has the same five files: the Autodesk Fusion electronics design (.f3z); the schematic (.sch) and board layout (.brd) in EAGLE format, which Fusion opens and KiCad can import; a bill of materials (BOM) spreadsheet with every part and its part number; and a ZIP of the Gerber and drill files a PCB manufacturer needs.

To have boards made, upload the Gerber ZIP to a PCB manufacturer's website and order the parts on the BOM. Then solder the parts yourself, or use the manufacturer's assembly service; the ZIP also includes pick-and-place files for that.

overview: ASCEND’s science plan connects measurements near the surface with observations higher in the atmosphere. Teams will investigate how smoke layers, atmospheric conditions, and terrain relate to air quality downwind.

The work includes sensor evaluation, comparison of surface and airborne observations, and analysis alongside NASA datasets. The aim is to understand both the atmosphere and the limits of the instruments used to measure it.

All ASCEND teams will collect air-quality data with the ASCEND Logger: a small PCB with GPS, pressure, temperature, and humidity sensors and an I2C port for a PM2.5 sensor. UAS and balloon teams fly it on their platforms; radiosonde teams may run it as a ground station. Guides for setting up, mounting, and using the Logger are in development.

title: High-Altitude Ballooning
description: Use radiosondes and student-integrated balloon payloads to investigate atmospheric structure and the vertical distribution of smoke.

subsections.title: Scientific Investigations
subsections.description: Investigate vertical smoke layers, gaps in remote-sensing observations, and transport near the tropopause.

overview: Small meteorological balloons with radiosondes provide profiles of temperature, pressure, humidity, and wind. Larger high-altitude balloons support student-integrated payloads for particulate measurements and other observations through a deeper atmospheric column.
ASCEND plans to combine these observations with UAS and surface measurements. Shared sensing, data logging, and comparison practices will help teams connect observations across platforms.

Balloon teams will use YELLOWSTONE, ASCEND’s LoRa tracking PCB, with its ground station program for flight tracking and flight termination. Air-quality and atmospheric data are recorded by the ASCEND Logger, the shared PCB every team flies.
